description: We are Team Expedition Nova, two AI/ML undergraduates from Bangladesh who love space science and interactive storytelling. Our project, Abandoned but Not Forgotten, is a 3D website built with Three.js that takes young explorers to 105 real machines NASA left on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space, with an X-ray view and stories told through NASA images. Next, we plan sharper 3D models and an AI guide that answers students’ questions as they explore.
summary:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive 3D website about the machines humanity has left across the solar system. Visitors begin with a view of the whole solar system and fly from Earth to the Moon, Mars, and deep space. At each stop they explore NASA hardware where it still is: retired satellites around Earth, Apollo landers and experiments on the Moon, silent rovers on Mars, and probes that ended at Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, or Saturn, or are leaving the Solar System.

The site covers 105 machines, built from NASA open data: mission records, archive photos, NASA 3D models, and NASA maps of Earth, the Moon, and Mars. Each machine has a 3D model, an X-ray view of its inside, a mission timeline, and a story told chapter by chapter by a friendly astronaut guide. Each story covers what the machine did, what became of it, and what we learned.

These machines are humanity’s footprints in space. Many still matter: Apollo’s mirrors still return lasers from Earth, and the Voyagers still send data from interstellar space. By turning scattered mission archives into one visual journey, the project makes space history easy for anyone to explore and to remember.
details:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is a scroll-driven 3D journey through the solar system to 105 machines NASA has left behind.

The journey: the homepage opens on the whole solar system. Scrolling, or the launch buttons, flies a rocket from Earth to the Moon, to Mars, and on to deep space. Glowing pins on Earth, the Moon and Mars mark real landing and crash sites, and clicking a planet opens the machines that ended their missions there.

Each destination page shows the machines one at a time, in 3D, where they rest:

  • on the Moon’s surface;
  • in the Martian dust;
  • on land or the seabed on Earth;
  • floating in space, with the planet, asteroid, or sun they ended at in the background.

For every machine, visitors can:

  • Turn the 3D model and look inside it with an “X-ray” lens
  • Read its key facts: launch, end of mission, where it is now, whether it still works, and introduce new words;
  • Browse NASA photos with credits;
  • Follow a chapter-by-chapter story told by an astronaut guide, from launch to what we learned.

Benefits

  • It brings scattered mission archives together in one place that’s easy to explore.
  • It explains complex missions in plain language for students, teachers, and the public.
  • It shows what happened to these machines after their missions ended, which most coverage skips.
  • It works in any modern browser, on computers and phones, with nothing to install.

Intended impact

  • Spark curiosity about space exploration and its history, especially among young people.
  • Raise awareness that our hardware stays out there, some of it still working (the Apollo laser mirrors, the Voyagers), and much of it silent.
  • Encourage people to explore NASA’s open data themselves.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: JavaScript, HTML, CSS; Python and Node.js for scripts that prepare the data and models.
    • NASA Science Visualization Studio maps of the Moon, Earth and the Milky Way;
    • Earth at Night (Black Marble);
    • Mars relief maps (MOLA and HRSC) via NASA Mars Trek;
    • NASA image archives and mission pages for the photos and facts.
  • Hosting: Vercel; code on GitHub.
  • Hardware: standard laptops and phones for development and testing.

What makes it creative?

  • It’s built as one continuous flight, not a list of pages.
  • Each machine is shown in its real setting.
  • A black-hole transition carries visitors between the journey and the destination pages.
  • The X-ray lens shows what’s inside each machine.
  • An astronaut guide tells each machine’s story.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: every fact and photo comes from NASA or partner sources and is credited. We note where the models are approximate and where distances are not to scale.
  • Accessibility: keyboard controls and screen-reader labels, support for reduced motion, and a fallback page for browsers without 3D (WebGL).
  • Performance: compressed models and texture sizes chosen to suit the device, so it runs on phones.
  • Usability: the layout adapts to both phones and desktops.
  • Licensing: NASA’s media usage guidelines were followed, and a full credits file lists every source.
